title: Complaint from 2611.06545: ledger-adjudicated labels still need an LLM reader and the true rate is a lower bound
abstract: Even with a per-task permission ledger as ground truth, the census of unsupported policy sentences in compaction summaries could not be automated and its rate is only a floor: 'Only rule-flagged summaries were read' and 'the rule labeler's recall is unknown'; the labeler's flags confirmed at 39 of 289 (authorizations) and 76 of 235 (held-out restrictions), and 'The two AI readers are copies of one model, so their close agreement does not show accuracy' (author vs AI-confirmed Cohen's kappa 0.38 on 60 items).

title: Complaint from 2611.06545: the restriction replay is null and the two confounded explanations cannot be separated
abstract: The pre-specified sentence-neutralization test on unsupported restrictions did not reject the null (126/148 to 119/148, p = 0.58) and the paper cannot say why the development effect vanished: 'F4 fixed the compaction point, but most of its sources were still overgeneralized. Templates that vary the two independently would be needed to separate the explanations in Section 5.4'; the edit itself is not clean: 'the neutral edit also removes whatever else a target sentence says, such as a next step or a reported rejection, and the count-matched control often replaced the line that states the task'.

title: Complaint from 2611.06545: the harness compacts at a step or finish call and hides the request, unlike deployed agents
abstract: The compaction trigger and the successor's input are harness artefacts: 'Compaction at the finish call, which dominated held-out instances, is a property of our harness. Deployed agents compact when the context fills' and 'The successor also never sees the original request, which may make the summary more influential than in deployed agents'; the scoped-approval prompt fix 'is true there because every required approval is named in the rules or the request; where requirements are not written down, it could suppress needed requests, which we did not test'.

title: Complaint from 2611.06483: tight-budget collapse of RL agents is confounded with an unseen budget prompt
abstract: The RL-over-base gain vanishes at 25% of the turn cap, but the RL model was trained only with the cap written as $T_{\max}$ in its prompt while the base model never saw the prompt at all, and no run separates budget dependence from prompt shift: 'Budget-aware prompt template used during training and evaluation' (Table 2); 'Standard multi-turn agentic RL samples trajectories under a fixed maximum budget $T_{\max}$' (sec. 5.2). The missing control is Full-budget RL evaluated at tight $T$ with the budget line held at $T_{\max}$ or removed, and a turn-penalised arm, all at Qwen3-4B on the paper's four tasks.

title: Complaint from 2611.06483: step-quality decline is measured only where an oracle exists
abstract: The claim that multi-turn RL does not improve and can degrade single-step action quality rests on FrozenLake (exact $Q^{*}$) and DeepCoder-MT (unit-test pass rate) and on injected rather than natural error states: 'Strictly evaluating one-step quality is challenging because reliable process rewards remain difficult to obtain in agentic settings' (sec. 3.3); 'Both constructions serve as proxies rather than rigorous definitions of error states' (App. B.5); 'even a strong judge model cannot consistently provide high-quality process supervision across all tasks, particularly in more realistic settings such as BFCL' (App. B.6).

title: Complaint from 2611.06483: the budget sweep is read at Pass@8, never at Pass@1, with no intervals
abstract: Every budget result is a coverage number over eight samples while the deployment risk invoked is single-attempt with irreversible actions: 'we fix the sampling breadth at $k=8$ and vary the maximum interaction turns $T$' (sec. 3.2); Table 1 is '$\mathrm{Pass}@T$ evaluation results ($\mathrm{Pass}@8$, %)'. $\mathrm{Pass}@(1,T)$, instance counts and confidence intervals for the sweep are not in the text, so whether RL's shrinking gap at tight $T$ is lost turns or lost sample diversity is undetermined.

title: Complaint from 2611.04399: generality of the four mechanisms is asserted, not surveyed
abstract: I audited two leaderboards and I am asking you to believe the class is everywhere on the strength of the mechanism alone: 'Our evidence comes from two leaderboards and the benchmarks they host, and the expectation that similar errors are common elsewhere rests on the mechanisms in Section 4 rather than on a survey.' (sec. 8); 'The expectation is an argument from mechanism.' (sec. 4). Nobody has counted how many public agent leaderboards gate grading on termination, nest tracing spans, replay gold through the agent's environment or re-grade across evaluator versions.

title: Complaint from 2611.04399: offline re-grade stubs the user simulator; benchmark owners silent on whether an unsolicited close is an ending
abstract: My offline re-grade of the ungraded half runs with the simulated user removed, so it scores the database and the output rule and nothing a user would have said or asked: 'The HAL re-grades use the τ-bench commit HAL's setup pins with the user simulator stubbed, so they evaluate the database and output criteria only.' (sec. 8). And the benchmark owners have not told me whether an unsolicited closing message is an ending or a failure: 'As of 3 November 2026 the τ-bench issue and the τ2-bench issue have no maintainer reply' (sec. 3.5).

title: Complaint from 2611.04399: instrument shifts have a direction but no size against run noise (one or two runs per cell)
abstract: I can give you the direction of the shift and not its size against run noise, because every cell is one or two runs: 'A model's cell holds one or two runs of about 41 records each, so the per-model gaps that end within a few points of zero are not resolved by these data, and the claim we rest on them is the direction of the shift.' (sec. 3.2). My own earlier paper measured a harness swap flipping as many tasks as a rerun (13%, 2610.04433) and this paper never puts the instrument terms it found on that scale.

title: Complaint from 2611.08453: no pre-run test of whether a teacher will distill
abstract: Practitioners pay the full distillation FLOPs before learning the teacher was wrong: 'Given an arbitrary LLM, there is currently no way to predict whether it will function as a stable OPD teacher without running the distillation. Developing such a diagnostic remains an open problem.' The paper's own first-batch top-16 overlap and its Appendix H spectral distance (three orders of magnitude between teachers that transfer and those that do not) are reported as side analyses, not as a gate.

title: Complaint from 2611.08453: FLOP-only ledger hides wall-clock, memory and the teacher's own cost
abstract: The 50x is a distillation-stage FLOP ratio at G=1 vs GRPO's G=8; the G=1 run 'takes longer in wall-clock time because it runs more optimizer steps', no wall-clock, GPU-hours or memory are reported for any pair, and 'The 50x ratio counts only distillation: the GRPO run has already produced the desired single domain model, so distilling it back into the base student adds cost.' The ledger is linear in tokens and parameters, so attention cost under length inflation (97.8% of external-teacher rollouts at the 30,720 cap) is uncounted.

title: Complaint from 2611.08453: only vanilla reverse-KL compared; student-over-teacher gain unexplained
abstract: The matched-FLOPs verdict covers one objective: 'Our study focuses on the vanilla reverse-KL OPD objective with a closed-form top-k estimator ... Recent work extends this baseline along axes we do not sweep at matched FLOPs ... Any of these may narrow the FLOPs gap we identify.' And the self-GRPO student exceeding its teacher by 11 points (Olmo-3-7B-Instruct-SFT, 51% vs 40%) is left with 'The cause for such substantial gap is unknown and left to future work.'

title: Complaint from 2611.05650: no pathwise replay certificate on hosted models
abstract: A frozen-state fork of a hosted frontier agent cannot be certified pathwise: 'three request payloads were each re-sent byte-identically with the same seed (four comparable call pairs across the three), and none reproduced its completion (0 of 4), while the serving path we controlled reproduced 34/34 calls and 2/2 episodes bitwise' (2611.05650 App. B.7); 'For hosted models the pathwise route may be unavailable' (sec. 5). The distributional route needs replicated continuations against an unedited-history live-vs-restored control with a prespecified margin, and no paper states an adequate margin or repeat count.

title: Complaint from 2611.05650: hash-identical snapshot is not the live run; model sensitivity unmeasured
abstract: A snapshot certified by five hash-identical clones still diverges from the live continuation because the random-stream position is not in the snapshot: clones 'agreed with one another in 24 of 24 states while differing from the live continuation in 9 and 20 of 24' (2611.05650 abstract); 'final-grader divergence under the oracle retry policy was 0/24 in every condition: an outcome-only metric would have hidden the problem, and whether realization-level infidelity moves model-driven behavior is unmeasured' (sec. 3.2). Every same-snapshot compaction probe forks a model at a boundary without this measurement.

title: Complaint from 2611.05650: the counterfactual standard has never been run; powered for sign only
abstract: The eight-arm history-manipulation design that would apply the standard is unrun: 'The design proposed in the second agenda item has never been run: every quantity below is a design parameter, not a result' (2611.05650 App. D); at 288 paired states x 3 repetitions the minimum detectable effect is '8–10 points' and 'as sized, the design is powered for the sign of the primary contrasts, not for the margins' (App. D.4). History-attribution results at the sizes compaction papers run are sign-only.

title: Complaint from 2611.03289: a label-free gate for when spreading retrieval is free
abstract: Varying retrieval size and filling part of each set with least-retrieved memories is the only way a deployed agent's log can determine memory values, but it costs accuracy where top-k already found the evidence, and the one rule that removes the cost needs gold labels: 'the only rule that removes the cost is an oracle that needs gold labels' (H.4); 'Finding at query time the questions where spreading retrieval costs nothing is the open problem that remains.' (sec. 6). The pre-registered substitute (top-1 similarity below median) failed its rule.

title: Complaint from 2611.03289: real-log memory values are additive and associational
abstract: Every memory value reported on a real log assumes no two memories help only together and that retrieval did not select on the query: 'the real-data experiments use $d=1$. Omitted dividends bias the estimates wherever they correlate with the design' and 'The reported values are associational unless the log is exogenous' (H.4); at $d=2$ the design has about $4.4\times10^{6}$ columns against $T=7{,}200$ episodes, so pairwise memory interactions are unmeasurable on real stores.

title: Complaint from 2611.03289: intervals unchecked on real logs; remedy failed to transfer
abstract: The confidence intervals on determined values are validated only where ground truth exists: 'Coverage of the intervals is measured on synthetic logs drawn from the model, where the true values are known; on real logs it cannot be measured.' (H.4), and the $d=2$ coverage headline is post hoc. The pre-registered transfer of the remedy to audited benchmarks 'failed: 0.46, 0.13, 0.08; falsified on MemoryAgentBench' and 'Reach is the binding ceiling' 'failed on two of three benchmarks' (Table 13); the real-data retention test 'was not completed' (F.7).

title: Complaint from 2611.08417: audit tool graded against the release it helped write
abstract: The continuous-validation workflow's accuracy is measured only against the Terminal-Bench 2.1 release it helped construct, so its true defect-discovery rate is unknown: 'Against the final TB2.1 release, the workflow reaches 57.1% precision and 71.4% recall. Because the workflow contributed to constructing the repair set, these metrics measure retrospective agreement with the release rather than independent defect discovery' (sec. 4); 'Agreement measures consistency rather than correctness.' (sec. 4). The one independent review (Harbor-Index, sec. 7) found misses: 'an incorrect reference answer in Lab-Bench, nondeterministic grading in QCircuitBench, and an HLE instruction admitting two plausible correct answers.'

title: Complaint from 2611.08417: a quarter of trials dropped, per-cell counts unreported, no replicate floor under rank moves
abstract: The TB2.0-to-TB2.1 paired re-score of 19 agents filters infrastructure failures before computing anything and never reports the per-cell trial count, so the reported up-to-three-rank moves carry no single-version re-run spread: 'However, we note that these filtered infrastructure trials account for roughly 27% of upstream trials.' (App. C.2); 'Timed-out trials are still graded on the state the agent left, and 11.8% of graded timeouts pass.' (App. C.2); $n_{a,t}$ is defined in sec. 3 and never given (Table 7 granularity suggests about 60 pooled trials per task across 19 entries).

title: Complaint from 2611.08417: the default time cap is arbitrary, moves harness gaps by 20 pp, and the sweep was unaffordable beyond six pairs
abstract: The paper shows a fixed wall-clock budget changes which harness looks better by about 20 pp on GPT 5.4 but has no principled rule for setting it and could sweep it on only a subset of agents: 'Owing to cost, this condition is run on a subset of the agents.' (sec. 3); 'An alternative would be to tune resource budgets per task. However, doing so would require repeated sweeps over any resource and would introduce an additional subjective design choice into the process.' (sec. 4); 'The results here show that a fixed resource budget is an arbitrary operating point and that the choice is not innocuous: it can change efficiency conclusions for individual models.' (sec. 6.2).

title: Complaint from 2611.02543: metastable cache trap shown only for PD-disaggregated SGLang on one hybrid MoE; full controller simulation-only
abstract: The surge-induced prefix-cache trap and the Basin controller are demonstrated on one model and one engine topology, and the complete predictor-driven policy exists only in a simulator that misses some baselines by 2.6x: 'All hardware experiments serve the hybrid MoE model Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on SGLang.' and 'In colocated deployments, prefill and decode share compute and memory; the corresponding model bounds would reflect that shared resource pool.' (sec. 9); 'The hardware prototype uses arrival-time ordering and current-context admission (§6.6); the predictor-driven controller is evaluated in simulation from §7.3 on.' (sec. 7.2). Whether colocated engines, RL rollout workers (verl/SGLang) or a full-attention model show the same trap is unshown.

title: Complaint from 2611.02543: peak-context admission runs on a weak text regression; the harness knows the answer and is never asked
abstract: Basin reserves each session's peak context from a ridge regression on task text with rank correlation 0.56-0.64, and the paper's own oracle shows exact peaks would add 1.27-1.35x goodput: 'The predictor uses the task text and first-prompt length visible at that call (§6.5).' (sec. 6.1); 'Supplying exact peak contexts raises goodput by 1.27–1.35 $\times$ in the plotted scenarios and 1.10–1.51 $\times$ across triggers, showing further benefit from improved predictions.' (sec. 7.9). The agent harness holds the turn cap, compaction rule and next tool duration ($K$ and $g$ in eq. 1) and no interface passes them to the gateway.

title: Complaint from 2611.02543: independent sessions and fixed capacity assumed; multi-agent workflows and autoscaling out of scope
abstract: The model and controller assume sessions that do not share lifetimes or pages and a cliff that does not move between profiles: 'The evaluated trajectories consist of independent sessions. Parent–child workflows couple their lifetimes: a parent can retain context while its child waits for service.' and 'These workflows therefore call for dependency-aware ordering, admission and prefix accounting.' (sec. 9); 'Basin assumes fixed capacity between profiles. Adding [42], switching or losing an instance changes the cliff, with new cache capacity becoming useful only as it warms.' (sec. 9).

title: The turn cap is a censoring time, not a failure: split Pass@(1,T) into a success curve, a wrong-commit curve and a still-running share, and read the RL-versus-base gap at tight budgets off the full-budget rollouts
abstract: In reliability engineering a life test stopped at a fixed time $T$ produces Type I censored data: units still running at $T$ are not failures, their failure time is only known to lie beyond $T$, and when a unit can fail in several ways the modes are competing risks, analysed one mode at a time with the other modes treated as censoring and recombined through the cumulative incidence function $\mathrm{CIF}_k(t) = \Pr(\tau \le t, D = k)$, never through the complement of a Kaplan-Meier curve, which overstates each mode when competing events exceed about 10% (Austin, Lee and Fine 2016). Carried into L2, that says a multi-turn rollout cut off at a turn cap $T$ is censored, not failed; a verified success at turn $\tau$ and a wrong commit (a submitted wrong answer or a terminal failure state) before $T$ are two competing event types; $\mathrm{Pass}@(1,T)$ is $\mathrm{CIF}_S(T)$; and because a policy that cannot see the cap behaves identically under every cap, the whole curve $\mathrm{CIF}_S(t)$ for $t \le T_{\max}$ is a free by-product of the full-budget rollouts, so the difference between $\mathrm{Pass}@(1,T)$ measured by actually running under cap $T$ with the cap in the prompt and $\widehat{\mathrm{CIF}}_S(T)$ read off the full-budget rollouts is exactly the budget-prompt effect that card 2611.06483 leaves confounded with budget need. Pre-registered: the RL model's deficit at a quarter of the cap is mostly still-running rollouts, not wrong commits, and the Full-budget RL model, which never trained with a tight counter in its prompt, shows a negative prompt gap that the base model does not.

sentences: A reliability test run for a fixed time $T$ on $n$ units gives Type I (right) censored data: $r$ exact failure times $t_1, \ldots, t_r$ are observed and $n - r$ units 'survived the entire $T$-hour test without failing', with $T$ fixed in advance and $r$ random; the failure times 'to the right (i.e., larger than $T$) are missing', not zero, and the estimators that handle this (Kaplan-Meier, hazard plotting, maximum likelihood) count a survivor as a run-time, never as a failure (NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook sec. 8.1.3.1).

When a unit can fail in $k$ different ways the failure modes are competing risks: each mode $i$ has its own life distribution $F_i(t)$ and hazard $h_i(t)$, the modes 'are having a race to see which can reach failure first', the unit fails at the first one, and under independence $R_c(t) = \prod_i R_i(t)$ and $h_c(t) = \sum_i h_i(t)$; each mode is analysed separately 'considering failures due to all other modes as censored run times' (e-Handbook sec. 8.1.8.1), where $R_c(t) = 1 - F_c(t)$ is the unit's reliability and $h_i(t)$ is the instantaneous rate of mode $i$ among units still running at $t$.

The crude probability of a specific event type by time $t$ is the cumulative incidence function $\mathrm{CIF}_k(t) = \Pr(\tau \le t, D = k)$, where $\tau$ is the event time and $D$ the event type; the CIFs of all types add up to the incidence of any event, and 'when estimating the crude incidence of outcomes, analysts should use the cumulative incidence function, rather than the complement of the Kaplan-Meier survival function', because treating competing events as censored 'results in estimates of incidence that are biased upward, regardless of whether the competing events are independent' (6.2 points in their heart-failure case), and 'absolute percentages of competing events of >10% merit serious consideration' (Austin, Lee and Fine 2016, Circulation 133:601-609).
sources: https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/apr/section1/apr131.htm — NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, sec. 8.1.3.1 'Censoring' (fetched 2026-11-08; Type I and Type II censoring, multicensored data, 'consider all failures due to modes other than the one being analyzed as censoring times')

https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/apr/section1/apr181.htm — NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook sec. 8.1.8.1 'Competing risk model' (fetched 2026-11-08; the three assumptions, the product and sum formulas, the race picture)

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4741409/ — Austin, Lee and Fine (2016), 'Introduction to the Analysis of Survival Data in the Presence of Competing Risks', Circulation 133(6):601-609 (fetched 2026-11-08; CIF definition, Kaplan-Meier upward bias, the 10% rule of thumb, cause-specific versus subdistribution hazards)

import_sentence: In reliability engineering, a test stopped at a fixed time produces censored units (still running, failure time unknown) and competing failure modes are analysed one at a time with the others treated as censored and recombined through the cumulative incidence function $\mathrm{CIF}_k(t) = \Pr(\tau \le t, D = k)$ rather than the complement of a Kaplan-Meier curve; carried into L2, that says an agent rollout cut at a turn cap $T$ is censored, not failed, a verified success and a wrong commit are two competing event types, $\mathrm{Pass}@(1,T) = \mathrm{CIF}_S(T)$, and for a policy that cannot see the cap the whole success curve $\mathrm{CIF}_S(t)$, $t \le T_{\max}$, is a free by-product of the full-budget rollouts, so the gap $\Delta(T) = \mathrm{Pass}@(1,T)^{\mathrm{run}} - \widehat{\mathrm{CIF}}_S^{\mathrm{full}}(T)$ between actually running under cap $T$ with the counter in the prompt and reading the full-budget curve at $T$ is the budget-prompt effect that 2611.06483 leaves confounded with budget need, and the three-way split (success, wrong commit, still running) says what RL changed.

predicts.statement: Setup: a task set, a policy $\pi$ (base or RL), a cap $T$. Each rollout ends at turn $\tau \le T$ with type $D \in \{S, C, R\}$: $S$ = success verified at turn $\tau$; $C$ = a wrong commit, that is a submitted wrong answer or a terminal failure state reached before the cap; $R$ = still running when the cap fires (censored). $\mathrm{Pass}@(1,T) = \Pr(\tau \le T, D = S) = \mathrm{CIF}_S(T)$; the wrong-commit curve is $\mathrm{CIF}_C(T)$; the still-running share is $1 - \mathrm{CIF}_S(T) - \mathrm{CIF}_C(T)$. From rollouts run at the full cap $T_{\max}$ with no budget line in the prompt, $\widehat{\mathrm{CIF}}_S^{\mathrm{full}}(t)$ for every $t \le T_{\max}$ is the fraction of rollouts with a success by turn $t$ (exact event times, no censoring before $T_{\max}$, so a count suffices). $\mathrm{Pass}@(1,T)^{\mathrm{run}}$ is measured by running under cap $T$ with the paper's budget-aware prompt (cap and remaining turns announced). The budget-prompt gap is $\Delta_\pi(T) = \mathrm{Pass}@(1,T)^{\mathrm{run}}_\pi - \widehat{\mathrm{CIF}}_{S,\pi}^{\mathrm{full}}(T)$, which is $0$ by construction for a policy whose behaviour does not depend on the announced cap. P1 (the prompt gap): at $T = 0.25\,T_{\max}$ on FrozenLake and DeepCoder-MT with Qwen3-4B, $|\Delta_{\mathrm{base}}| < 3$ points while $\Delta_{\mathrm{RL\text{-}Full}} \le -5$ points (the Full-budget RL model only ever saw $T_{\max}$ in its prompt). P2 (what RL changed): at every $T$, $\mathrm{CIF}_{C,\mathrm{RL}}(T) \le \mathrm{CIF}_{C,\mathrm{base}}(T)$ (RL commits wrong less, the paper's error-recovery finding restated as a hazard), and at $0.25\,T_{\max}$ at least 60% of the RL-minus-base deficit in $\widehat{\mathrm{CIF}}_S^{\mathrm{full}}$ is still-running mass, not wrong-commit mass. P3 (the reporting bias): the conditional success rate among non-censored rollouts, $\mathrm{CIF}_S(T) / (\mathrm{CIF}_S(T) + \mathrm{CIF}_C(T))$, the number a leaderboard reports when it drops timeouts from the denominator (card 2611.04399's graded fraction; 2611.08417's 'over half of failed trials at default budget are timeouts'), overstates $\mathrm{CIF}_S(T)$ by more for RL than for base at tight $T$, so the RL-over-base ordering at $0.25\,T_{\max}$ flips between the two conventions on at least one of the two tasks.
predicts.expected: Judgment, not evidence: probability 0.5 that P1 holds as stated (negative RL prompt gap of 5 points or more with a near-zero base gap); 0.2 that the RL gap is positive (the counter makes it hurry); 0.3 that both gaps are under 3 points. Probability 0.6 that P2 holds (the tight-budget deficit is mostly censored mass). Probability 0.4 that P3's ordering flip appears on at least one task. Expected mechanism: outcome-only RL at a fixed cap lowers the wrong-commit hazard and shifts success later (it learns to keep trying), which is invisible at the full cap and reads as a loss under truncation; the budget counter is a prompt the Full-budget model never trained on, and part of BudgetMix's gain is prompt-distribution matching rather than budget sampling.
predicts.field_assumes: 2611.06483 reads the sweep as 'trajectory-level RL advantages depend on sufficient turn budgets' and scores a rollout cut at $T$ as a failure identical to a wrong commit ($\mathrm{Pass}@(K,T)$ is the probability that at least one of $K$ trajectories cut at $T$ is scored 1); its prompt announces the cap and remaining turns at every step, so a tight-budget evaluation is a new prompt and a truncation at once, and the paper never runs the separating control (card 2611.06483, load_bearing_assumption). The evaluation-statistics line that already treats the cap as censoring (DAPRO 2605.06605, HARP 2610.07362: 'interactions may be terminated before the event occurs, so that event times are only partially observed (censored)') has one event of interest and no competing event, and is about allocating an evaluation budget, not about what RL changed. The reliability-engineering assumption is the opposite of the paper's: a unit still running at the end of the test is not a failure, and a wrong commit is a different mode from running out of time.
predicts.belief_changing: If P1 holds, the headline 'RL gains depend on sufficient interaction budget' is partly a prompt artifact: the budget-aware line (BudgetMix, AnySearch 2609.00813, On the Clock 2610.10833) must report the no-counter curve beside the counter curve, and the cheapest fix for deployment at unknown caps is to drop the counter rather than to retrain. If P1 fails and P2 holds, the mechanism is 'RL learned to take longer and commit wrong less', the evaluation fix is to report the three-way split with the cap as a censoring line, and BudgetMix is the right recipe for a known deployment cap. If P3 holds, every leaderboard that drops timeouts or ungraded runs from its denominator is publishing a Kaplan-Meier-style overstatement, which changes a ruler across L1 (tau-bench max-turns, Terminal-Bench wall-clock caps, HAL graded fraction).

identifiability: Random given: a fixed task set and seed-fixed environments (FrozenLake maps are generated and train/test disjoint; DeepCoder-MT unit tests are deterministic), a fixed policy checkpoint, fixed sampling settings (the paper evaluates at temperature 0.6, top-$p$ 0.9), and a fixed cap and prompt. The event time $\tau$ and type $D$ are then random through the policy's sampling only; at temperature 0 in a deterministic environment there is one trajectory per task and the curves are step functions over tasks, which is still a valid CIF over the task population but has no within-task variance, so $n \ge 8$ samples per task at the harness temperature are required for the per-task hazards and the record states $n$ and the temperature. Whose property: $\mathrm{CIF}_S$ and $\mathrm{CIF}_C$ are properties of the (policy, sampling, environment) system; $\Delta_\pi(T)$ is a property of the policy's response to the prompt and is $0$ for any policy whose actions do not read the cap, which is the identity that makes the full-budget curve a valid control for a budget-blind policy and makes a non-zero gap attributable to the counter. The competing-risks independence assumption of the NIST model is not needed: the CIFs are crude probabilities estimated by counting, and the only claim that depends on independence (a cause-specific hazard interpreted as 'what success would be if wrong commits were impossible') is not made. Protocol terms: what counts as a wrong commit is defined per environment in advance (DeepCoder-MT: a submission that fails the hidden tests and is the final action; FrozenLake: falling into a hole; BFCL/InterCode: a final answer that the checker rejects) and reported with its share; the conditional rate in P3 is a protocol artifact by construction and is shown only to expose it. Judge versus verifier: all event types come from the environment's verifier, no judge.

papers.title: Spend Where It Counts: Dynamic Budget Allocation for Multi-Turn LLM Evaluation (DAPRO); Dynamic Budget Allocation for LLM Evaluation under Hard Resource Constraints (HARP)
papers.trick: Treat the number of turns until an event (a jailbreak, a task completion) as a time-to-event that is censored when the interaction is stopped early, and allocate an evaluation budget across trajectories so that conformal lower bounds on the time-to-event keep coverage without exceeding the budget.

papers.title: Evaluation of Multi-Turn Consistency in LLM Agents: Survival Analysis and Failure-Rationale Taxonomy
papers.trick: In a 20-step delayed-gratification game, treat the first reward claim as the event, fit Kaplan-Meier curves and a discrete-time hazard regression across model families and manipulations, and code the rationales of agents that quit.
papers.did_not_do: The event is the failure itself (claiming early), there is no competing event type and no cap-as-censoring reading (every episode runs the full 20 steps unless it ends by the event), no RL training, no task verifier and no prompt-gap control. Fourth: 2610.10833 trains GRPO under wall-clock budgets and reports that multi-budget GRPO 'tends to collapse toward the strategy learned for the shortest budget', with no censoring treatment. title: A policy trained at a fixed turn cap with the counter in its prompt is a finite-horizon controller: test time-to-go invariance, and compare a terminal value at truncation against BudgetMix at matched compute
abstract: In optimal control a finite-horizon problem has a time-varying optimal policy, $u_i = \kappa_{N-i}(x)$: the action depends on the state and on the steps to go $N - i$, not on $N$ or $i$ separately (Rawlings, Mayne and Diehl 2017, sec. 2.3), and a receding-horizon controller is made consistent across horizons by a terminal cost $V_f$ that stands in for the cost beyond the horizon, chosen in practice as the infinite-horizon cost to go (their Assumption 2.14 and sec. 6.3); deep RL carries the same two options as Pardo et al. 2018: if the time limit is part of the task, add the remaining time to the input; if it is a training convenience, bootstrap from the value of the state where the episode was cut. Carried into L2, that says the policies in card 2611.06483 (cap and remaining turns announced in the prompt, trained at one cap, evaluated at others) are time-aware finite-horizon controllers specialised to their training cap, BudgetMix is horizon randomisation, and the frameworks' treatment of a rollout cut at the cap (reward 0, no terminal value) is the missing terminal cost; it predicts (i) that a budget-aware policy's action distribution at a matched state depends on turns-to-go alone, which no budget-aware paper tests and which 2610.10833's collapse to the shortest-budget strategy suggests fails, and (ii) that PPO with a bootstrapped terminal value at the cap and no counter in the prompt recovers at a quarter of the cap at least half of what BudgetMix recovers over Full-budget PPO.

sentences: Dynamic programming for a horizon-$N$ problem 'yields much more than an optimal control sequence for a given initial state; it yields an optimal feedback policy' $\{\kappa_N, \kappa_{N-1}, \ldots, \kappa_1\}$: 'at event $(x, i)$, i.e., at state $x$ at time $i$, the time to go is $N - i$ and the optimal control is $\kappa_i^0(x) = \kappa_{N-i}(x)$', so the optimal finite-horizon policy is time-varying through the steps that remain, and $V_j(x)$ is 'the optimal cost for problem $\mathbb{P}_j(x)$ if the current state is $x$, current time is $N - j$, and the terminal time is $N$' (Rawlings, Mayne and Diehl, Model Predictive Control, 2nd ed., sec. 2.3).

A receding-horizon controller that re-solves the horizon-$N$ problem at every step is stabilised by the 'basic stability assumption' on the terminal cost $V_f$ and terminal set $\mathbb{X}_f$: for every $x \in \mathbb{X}_f$ there is a $u$ with $f(x,u) \in \mathbb{X}_f$ and $V_f(f(x,u)) \le V_f(x) - \ell(x,u)$, where $\ell$ is the stage cost; under it the optimal value $V_N^0$ is a Lyapunov function and 'MPC cost is less than terminal cost' (Assumption 2.14, Propositions 2.18 and 2.35, sec. 2.4.2). The terminal cost is the stand-in for everything beyond the horizon, and the recommended choice is the long-run cost: 'we choose the terminal penalty to be the infinite horizon cost to go' (sec. 6.3, eq. 6.8).

The deep-RL carrier of the same distinction is Pardo, Tavakoli, Levdik and Kormushev (2018): when the agent must 'maximize its performance over that fixed period', 'the terminations due to time limits are in fact part of the environment, and thus a notion of the remaining time should be included as part of the agent's input to avoid violation of the Markov property'; when the time limits 'are only used during training to diversify experience', the fix is 'bootstrapping from the value of the state at the end of each partial episode', and treating the cut as terminal causes 'state aliasing and invalidation of experience replay, leading to suboptimal policies and training instability'.
sources: https://sites.engineering.ucsb.edu/~jbraw/mpc/MPC-book-2nd-edition-1st-printing.pdf — Rawlings, Mayne and Diehl (2017), Model Predictive Control: Theory, Computation, and Design, 2nd ed., Nob Hill (fetched 2026-11-08; sec. 2.3 dynamic programming solution and time to go, sec. 2.4.2 stabilizing conditions and Assumption 2.14, sec. 6.3 terminal penalty as infinite-horizon cost to go)

import_sentence: In optimal control, a finite-horizon problem has a time-varying optimal policy $u_i = \kappa_{N-i}(x)$ that depends on the steps to go, and a receding-horizon controller is made consistent across horizons by a terminal cost $V_f$ standing in for the cost beyond the horizon (chosen as the infinite-horizon cost to go); carried into L2, that says an agent trained at one turn cap with the cap and remaining turns in its prompt is a time-aware finite-horizon controller specialised to that cap (so its actions at a matched state should depend on turns-to-go alone, a testable invariance), BudgetMix is horizon randomisation, and scoring a rollout cut at the cap as a zero-reward terminal is a missing terminal cost whose fix, a bootstrapped terminal value at the cap with no counter in the prompt, should be compared against BudgetMix at matched compute before 'RL gains depend on the turn budget' is read as a property of what RL learns.

predicts.statement: Setup: FrozenLake from 2611.06483 ($T_{\max} = 70$, Qwen3-4B; DeepCoder-MT, $T_{\max} = 10$, if budget allows), the paper's VeRL recipe. P0 (zero GPU, the framework fact): in VeRL multi-turn and in the paper's pinned BudgetMix adapter, a rollout that reaches the turn cap is marked done with terminal reward 0 and no bootstrapped value (PPO's GAE treats $s_{T_{\max}}$ as terminal; GRPO assigns the group-relative advantage of a 0 to every token of the truncated trajectory); and the share $q$ of Full-budget training rollouts that end by the cap is reported (it sets how much any truncation fix can matter). P1 (time-to-go invariance): for a BudgetMix policy, at matched states $s$ sampled from its own trajectories, the action distribution under prompt condition (cap $B_1$, used $u_1$) and (cap $B_2$, used $u_2$) with $B_1 - u_1 = B_2 - u_2$ agrees (total variation over 16 sampled actions, averaged over 200 states) within the agreement of two draws at the identical prompt, while conditions with equal cap and different turns-to-go disagree by at least twice that; a Full-budget policy shows no such structure. P2 (terminal value versus horizon randomisation): PPO with partial-episode bootstrapping at the cap (the critic's $V_\phi(s_{T_{\max}})$ as the terminal value) and no budget line in the prompt, evaluated at $T = 0.25\,T_{\max}$ with no budget line, recovers at least half of the gap that BudgetMix-PPO closes over Full-budget PPO at that cap (the paper's Table 1 reports BudgetMix gains averaged over algorithms; the PPO-only gap is measured here), at matched optimizer steps and rollout budget. P3: the cheap critic-free stand-in for GRPO, masking cap-truncated trajectories out of the group advantage (DAPO's overlong filtering carried from tokens to turns), recovers less than PEB-PPO does.
predicts.expected: Judgment, not evidence: probability 0.9 that P0 holds (the frameworks treat the cap as terminal; the share $q$ is unknown, expected 10-40% on FrozenLake at $T_{\max} = 70$). Probability 0.35 that P1's invariance holds for BudgetMix (2610.10833's collapse to the shortest-budget strategy and AnySearch's need for a two-phase scaffold both suggest learned budget awareness is not a clean function of turns-to-go). Probability 0.45 that P2 holds (PEB recovers at least half of BudgetMix's PPO gain at a quarter of the cap). Probability 0.5 for P3. Expected mechanism: a zero terminal at the cap teaches the policy that long trajectories are bad only when they are cut, which at the full cap is rare, so the trained policy spreads its work over the budget; a terminal value says how close the cut rollout was, which is the information a tight-budget deployment needs.
predicts.field_assumes: 2611.06483 fixes the budget dependence by training on sampled caps with the counter in the prompt ('sample the training budget uniformly from ten fractions of the cap', card) and reads the tight-budget loss as a property of what RL learned; AnySearch 2609.00813 injects 'explicit budget state' and samples budgets; On the Clock 2610.10833 injects timing information and trains GRPO with budget-aware rewards. All three take Pardo's case (i) (time-awareness) and none examines case (ii) (bootstrap at the cut) or asks what the framework does at the cap; the DAPO precedent (mask truncated responses) exists at the token level only. The control-theory assumption is that a finite-horizon policy is a function of turns-to-go and that horizon consistency comes from the terminal cost, not from randomising the horizon.
predicts.belief_changing: If P2 holds, budget dependence is partly a truncation-handling artifact of the de facto frameworks and the recipe change is one line (bootstrap at the cap, drop the counter), which every multi-turn RL paper evaluated at tight budgets must then control for; BudgetMix's gain is re-read as horizon randomisation plus prompt matching. If P2 fails (PEB recovers under a quarter of the gain), the finite-horizon mechanism is refuted for these tasks, the tight-budget loss is learned pacing, and the time-awareness route (BudgetMix, AnySearch) is the right one, with P1 then saying whether the learned awareness is the clean turns-to-go function control theory predicts or a cap-specific behaviour that will not transfer to unseen caps.

identifiability: Random given: fixed tasks and seed-fixed FrozenLake maps, fixed base checkpoint, fixed recipe and optimizer-step budget per arm, fixed sampling at training (temperature 1.0) and evaluation (0.6). P0 is a code fact, not a measurement. P1 compares action distributions at a matched state under two prompts: at temperature 0 both are deterministic and the 'agreement' is a 0/1 match with no distribution, so the test uses 16 sampled actions at the training temperature and the within-prompt replicate agreement as the null, and the record states both; the quantity is a property of the (policy, prompt template) pair, not of the environment. P2 and P3 compare training arms at matched compute; a single seed per arm is the paper's own practice and the W44 lesson says it is not enough, so the probe runs two seeds per arm on FrozenLake and reports the between-seed spread beside the between-arm difference; an arm difference inside the seed spread is reported as inconclusive, not as a result. Whose property: the terminal value $V_\phi(s_{T_{\max}})$ is the critic's estimate and its error is part of the arm, so P2 is a statement about the PEB-PPO recipe as run, not about the ideal terminal cost. Protocol terms: the cap fraction (0.25) and the matched-state sample (200 states) are choices; the full cap sweep is reported. Judge versus verifier: all outcomes are from the environment's verifier; no judge.

probe.design: Step 0 ($0, one day): read VeRL's multi-turn rollout and advantage code and the paper's pinned adapter (github.com/GaryStack/Rethinking-Agent-RL, docs/tutorials/budgetmix.md) to establish how a cap-reached rollout is terminated and credited; write P0 with file and line. Step 1 (about 40 GPU-hours): train Full-budget GRPO and BudgetMix GRPO on FrozenLake with Qwen3-4B (the paper's recipe, $G = 16$), then run the P1 matched-state test (200 states x 2 prompt pairs x 16 actions, inference only, about 2 GPU-hours) on both; the Full-budget run is shared with import:2026-W45-S8xF9 if both run the same week. Step 2 (about 120 GPU-hours, two seeds per arm, FrozenLake, Qwen3-4B or 1.7B if the budget binds): PPO x {terminal-zero, partial-episode bootstrapping at the cap} x {counter in prompt, no counter}, plus BudgetMix-PPO with counter, all at matched optimizer steps and rollouts; evaluate every arm at $T \in \{0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1\} T_{\max}$ under its own prompt convention with 8 samples per task; report $\mathrm{Pass}@(1,T)$ and $\mathrm{Pass}@(8,T)$ with task-cluster bootstrap intervals and the seed spread. Step 3 (optional, about 20 GPU-hours): GRPO with cap-truncated trajectories masked from the group advantage, for P3.

title: A handoff summary is a state estimate that passes the mean and drops the covariance, so the successor's gain on new evidence is zero: already made (verification-status laundering, Agent-BRACE, Reclaim)
abstract: In state estimation an estimate is a pair (mean, covariance), the receiver of an estimate updates it on a new measurement $y$ with the gain $L = Q C^\top (C Q C^\top + R)^{-1}$, where $Q$ is the prior covariance, $R$ the measurement noise and $C$ the measurement map, and an estimate handed over with $Q = 0$ has gain $0$: the receiver never revises it however loud the evidence (Rawlings, Mayne and Diehl 2017, sec. 1.4.2). Carried into L4, that says a compaction or handoff summary that carries the writer's claims without the writer's uncertainty (hedges, verification status, the number of observations behind each entry) makes the successor treat guesses as facts, which is the mechanism behind card 2611.06545 (hedged guesses in reasoning reappear in summaries as rules) and behind the W44 import's 'the compacted agent cannot overwrite what it reads as fact'. The import is already made: 2609.20211 shows summarizers 'weaken the status' and memory compressors 'remove it', with risky-action approval rising from 5% to 60% when the unverified framing is stripped, and proposes carrying 'authorization provenance as structured state attached to the claim'; 2605.11436 (Agent-BRACE) carries each belief claim with an ordinal verbalized certainty label as the compact state; 2606.25449 (Reclaim) shows a memory that keeps a conclusion and drops its derivation re-emits the stale value as a confident answer and prescribes keeping the recomputable source. The one F4 piece none of them has, that carried uncertainty must inflate with time since the last observation ($P^- = A P A^\top + W$, the forecast step), is the relaxation-time axis already filed as import:2026-W44-S3xF11, so nothing is filed here.

sentences: Given a prior $x_0 \sim N(\bar x_0, Q_0)$ and a measurement $y_0 = C x_0 + v_0$ with noise $v_0 \sim N(0, R)$, the conditional density of the state is normal with mean $m = \bar x_0 + L_0 (y_0 - C \bar x_0)$ and gain $L_0 = Q_0 C^\top (C Q_0 C^\top + R)^{-1}$, and covariance $P_0 = Q_0 - Q_0 C^\top (C Q_0 C^\top + R)^{-1} C Q_0$; 'the variance after measurement, $P_0$, is always less than or equal to $Q_0$, which implies that we can only gain information by measurement; but the information gain may be small if the measurement device is poor and the measurement noise variance $R$ is large' (Rawlings, Mayne and Diehl, sec. 1.4.2). Reading the gain the other way: as the prior covariance $Q_0 \to 0$ the gain $L_0 \to 0$ and the measurement is ignored, so an estimate passed on as certain is never corrected.

Between measurements the estimate is propagated through the model $x_{k+1} = A x_k + w_k$ with process noise $w_k \sim N(0, W)$ (the book writes $Q$ for this covariance; $W$ is used here to keep it apart from the prior covariance $Q_0$), and the covariance grows: $P^-_{k+1} = A P_k A^\top + W$; the book notes that when the state is subjected to large disturbances this covariance is large, so a carried estimate becomes less trustworthy with every step on which it was not re-observed, and the receiver's gain rises accordingly (same section, 'Forecasting the state evolution').

The same book's Exercise 1.42 ('Least squares parameter estimation and Bayesian estimation') makes the two limits explicit: it asks the reader to show that Bayesian and least-squares estimation 'give the same result in the limit of an infinite variance prior', that is, when 'the covariance of the prior is large compared to the covariance of the measurement error' the estimate is the measurement alone; at the other limit, a zero-variance prior, the estimate is the prior alone; the weight on new evidence is set entirely by the ratio of carried uncertainty to measurement noise.
sources: https://sites.engineering.ucsb.edu/~jbraw/mpc/MPC-book-2nd-edition-1st-printing.pdf — Rawlings, Mayne and Diehl (2017), Model Predictive Control, 2nd ed., sec. 1.4.1-1.4.2 'Linear optimal state estimation' (fetched 2026-11-08; the conditional-density update, the gain, the covariance decrease, the forecast step)

title: The compressor is a gauge: separate the writer-stage repeatability of compaction harm (re-compact the same history) from the successor-stage repeatability (TRACE's split-half replicate) and from writer reproducibility, before any per-boundary harm label or history-based trigger is trusted
abstract: In metrology an instrument is characterised before it is trusted by a gauge study that separates repeatability (the same gauge reading the same artifact repeatedly), reproducibility (different operators, days or gauges on the same artifact), stability and bias against a reference, in a nested design whose pooled level-1 and level-2 standard deviations say how much a single reading can be believed and how many repeats a reported value needs (NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook ch. 2.4). Carried into L4, that says a compaction compressor is a gauge that reads a history and emits a summary, and the per-boundary harm numbers the lane now builds on (TRACE's paired replay, SJC's 83% of failures traced to a summary entry, the corpus study's history-based triggers, 2611.06545's unsupported-policy census) are single readings: one summary per boundary. The successor-stage repeatability is measured (2610.08722's split-half replicate: half-half correlation 0.40, replicate AUROC 0.72, with the summary held fixed), writer reproducibility is measured in pieces (2611.06545: 1.2% versus 2.4% unsupported restrictions by writer; HSC-Bench: receiver dependence), and the writer-stage repeatability, re-compacting the same history at the deployed sampling setting and continuing each summary, is measured nowhere. Pre-registered: the writer-stage component is at least a quarter of the harm variance (judgment 0.45), which caps any history-based trigger near the corpus study's 0.66 and says per-boundary labels need at least three re-compactions; if it is under a tenth, the writer is effectively deterministic and the corpus protocol stands.

sentences: A gauge study characterises 'the behavior of gauges in a particular environment with respect to: repeatability, reproducibility, stability, bias', and asks whether 'instruments in the same environment produce equivalent results', whether 'operators in the same environment produce equivalent results', and whether responses 'are affected by configuration or geometry changes or changes in setup procedures' (NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook sec. 2.4.1); its findings are incorporated 'in an uncertainty budget'.

Repeatability 'quantifies the basic precision for the gauge': a level-1 standard deviation $s_1$ is computed from $J$ repetitions of the same artifact under the same conditions and pooled over days, runs and check standards ('a repeatability standard deviation from $J$ repetitions is not a reliable estimate of the precision of the gauge', so pooling to $LK(J-1)$ degrees of freedom is the rule); reproducibility is the level-2 standard deviation $s_2$ of the per-day (or per-operator) averages, pooled over runs, in a nested design in which repetitions sit inside days inside runs (secs. 2.4.4.1-2.4.4.2). The two levels are separated because a reading's total spread is $s_1^2/J + s_2^2$ for an average of $J$ repeats, so the number of repeats that buys precision depends on which level dominates.

Biases are 'differences among gauges', 'differences among geometries, configurations' and 'operator biases', estimated against a reference or check standard and entered in the uncertainty budget as a maximum bias with an assumed distribution (sec. 2.4.6); a gauge study is 'the basis for uncertainty assessment' only 'if the results are truly representative of the measurement process in its working environment', and the study is repeated before and after when the process is suspected of changing.
sources: https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/mpc/section4/mpc41.htm — NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, sec. 2.4.1 'What are the important issues?' (fetched 2026-11-08)

import_sentence: In metrology an instrument is trusted only after a nested gauge study separates its repeatability (same artifact, repeated readings), its reproducibility (different operators or instruments on the same artifact) and its bias against a reference, with pooled level-1 and level-2 standard deviations that say how many repeats a reported value needs; carried into L4, that says a compaction compressor is a gauge that reads a history and emits a summary, the lane's per-boundary harm numbers are single readings, and before a harm label, a source gate or a history-based trigger is trusted, the writer-stage repeatability (re-compact the same history $m$ times at the deployed sampling setting, continue each) must be separated from the successor-stage repeatability (TRACE's split-half replicate, 0.40) and from writer reproducibility (2611.06545's 1.2% versus 2.4%), because a harm that varies as much across re-compactions of one history as across histories cannot be predicted from the history at all.

predicts.statement: Setup: $B \approx 150$ compaction boundaries from a public harness with re-executable state (2611.06545's handoff-audit harness, writer = agent model at the developers' sampling settings, Qwen3-8B at temperature 0.6 and gpt-oss-20b at 1.0; or SJC's AppWorld harness). At each boundary $b$, re-compact the same pre-compaction history $m = 4$ times at the writer's deployed setting (summaries $j = 1..m$), and continue each summary $n = 3$ times from the re-executed state (continuations $k = 1..n$). Harm $y_{bjk}$ is a judge-free outcome: TRACE's burden (errored or repeated calls among the next $K = 5$ actions) or 2611.06545's ledger-checked unsupported action. Nested model: $y_{bjk} = \mu + \alpha_b + \beta_{j(b)} + \epsilon_{k(bj)}$ with variance components $\sigma^2_B$ (between histories), $\sigma^2_W$ (writer: between summaries of one history) and $\sigma^2_E$ (successor: between continuations of one summary), estimated by nested ANOVA with a boundary-cluster bootstrap. P1 (writer repeatability): $\sigma^2_W / (\sigma^2_B + \sigma^2_W + \sigma^2_E) \ge 0.25$. Consequence written now: the reliability of a single-summary, $n$-continuation harm label is $\rho_1 = \sigma^2_B / (\sigma^2_B + \sigma^2_W + \sigma^2_E / n)$, and a predictor that reads only the history has its correlation with the label attenuated by $\sqrt{\rho_1}$, so the corpus study's 0.66 against a 0.72 replicate is read against this ceiling. P2 (reproducibility): with two writers on the same histories, the writer-by-history interaction component exceeds the writer main effect, so which writer is 'safer' depends on the history. P3 (bias): the per-writer unsupported-policy rate against the ledger (2611.06545's census) is a gauge bias, stable across re-compactions: the between-re-compaction variance of the flagged-sentence count per boundary is at or below its binomial value, so the rate is a writer property, not dice. Also reported: the writer-stage repeatability of the summary itself (length and entry overlap across the $m$ re-compactions), the statistic 2605.23296 saw fluctuate.
predicts.expected: Judgment, not evidence: probability 0.45 that P1 holds (writer share at least 0.25); 0.3 that it is between 0.10 and 0.25; 0.25 that it is under 0.10. Probability 0.4 for P2; 0.5 for P3. Expected mechanism: at the deployed temperature the writer's choice of which operations, values and next steps to keep varies across draws, and the W44 import's fast entries (plans, next steps) are the most variable; the successor acts on whichever draw it received, so harm inherits the writer's dice.
predicts.field_assumes: One summary per boundary is the summary: TRACE's corpus (590 boundaries, one summary each), SJC (per-entry source labels on one draw), HSC-Bench, 2611.06545 ($K = 4$ successor runs per arm, one summary per source), and the corpus study's triggers all treat the compressor as a deterministic function of the history; the corpus study's own replicate yardstick splits 'each boundary's PRE and POST rollouts into disjoint halves' with the summary fixed (2610.08722, App. F), so it measures the successor stage only, and the authors note that 'the same numbers also support an attenuation reading' without a stage split. 2605.23296 observed that 'the information it retains fluctuate[s] substantially from run to run, making the agent's retained knowledge unpredictable across runs' as a serving-control problem, with no harm measurement and no partition. The metrology assumption is the reverse: a reading is a draw from the gauge, and the gauge is characterised before its readings are compared.
predicts.belief_changing: If P1 holds, per-boundary harm labels need at least three re-compactions, the history-based trigger line is capped near where the corpus study found it, SJC's 83% entry attribution is a statement about one draw, CL-W44-06's census and deletion arms must average over writer draws, and compaction evaluations add a writer-replicate arm (a protocol change across the lane). If the writer share is under 0.10, the compressor is effectively deterministic at the deployed setting, the corpus protocol and TRACE's successor-only replicate are the right yardstick, and the result is a footnote that licenses single-summary labels. If P3 holds, the unsupported-policy rate is a calibratable writer bias (a column per writer model), not a per-run accident.

identifiability: Random given: fixed task, fixed pre-compaction history, deterministic re-executed state (2611.06545's synthetic environment replays from a snapshot; AppWorld is deterministic given the action sequence), fixed writer model, prompt and sampling, fixed successor model and sampling. The writer-stage component $\sigma^2_W$ is defined at the writer's deployed sampling setting: at temperature 0 on a deterministic server it is zero by construction and the design collapses to TRACE's successor-only replicate, so the record states the writer's temperature (0.6 and 1.0 in the handoff-audit harness, the developers' recommended settings) and reports $\sigma^2_W$ at that setting; a production compactor run at temperature 0 inherits only the serving-stack nondeterminism component (2602.07150), which is reported separately by running $m$ re-compactions at temperature 0 as a control arm. Whose property: $\sigma^2_W$ belongs to the (writer model, prompt, sampling) acting on that history; $\sigma^2_E$ to the (successor, sampling, environment); $\sigma^2_B$ to the task-and-history population, so the shares are reported per harness and the components, not only the shares. Protocol terms: $m$, $n$, the burden window $K$ and the harm definition are choices and are reported with a sensitivity row ($K = 3, 5, 8$). Judge versus verifier: harm is an executable label (errored or repeated call; ledger-checked write), never a judge; the summary-entry overlap uses exact normalised matching (2610.26836). The nested ANOVA assumes the writer draws are exchangeable within a boundary, which holds by construction when the $m$ re-compactions use identical inputs.

probe.design: Step 1 (about 15 GPU-hours, 7 days including 3 of harness work): on 2611.06545's released handoff-audit harness (MIT; vLLM; Qwen3-8B and gpt-oss-20b), take 150 compaction snapshots from the held-out templates, re-compact each 4 times at the developers' sampling settings, continue each summary 3 times for 8 successor steps, and score TRACE burden and the ledger-checked unsupported-action outcome; fit the nested model, bootstrap the components by boundary, and report the shares and $\rho_1$ with intervals, plus the summary-level repeatability (length, entry overlap). Step 2 (about 5 GPU-hours): the temperature-0 control arm (4 re-compactions at temperature 0 per boundary) to separate sampling variance from serving nondeterminism. Step 3 (about 10 GPU-hours): the second writer on the same 150 histories for P2 and the flagged-sentence counts per re-compaction for P3. Optional step 4 (about $400 API or 20 GPU-hours): the same design on SJC's AppWorld harness for one agent model, to check that the writer share is not a property of the synthetic tasks.
probe.dollars: about $100 at H100 spot rates for steps 1-3 (the paper's whole study cost about 48 GPU-hours); $400 more for the optional AppWorld replication
probe.days: 10 days: 3 of harness work, 3 of runs, 2 of analysis, 2 for the second writer
probe.kills_if: Dead as a claim if the writer share $\sigma^2_W / (\sigma^2_B + \sigma^2_W + \sigma^2_E)$ is under 0.10 with the bootstrap interval's upper end under 0.20 on both writers: the compressor is effectively deterministic at the deployed setting, single-summary labels are licensed, and the result is a protocol footnote. Also dead as a ruler if fewer than 100 of the 150 snapshots re-execute to an identical state (the replay certificate of 2611.05650), since then the successor component is contaminated by state drift.

consumers.class: Compaction evaluators (TRACE 2608.06503 and its corpus study 2610.08722, HSC-Bench 2610.36523, 2611.06545's replay protocol)
consumers.action_changed: Add a writer-replicate arm ($m \ge 3$ re-compactions per boundary) beside the successor replicate, report the nested components, and ship summary text with the corpus so the writer stage can be audited (the corpus study already asks what corpora should ship).

consumers.class: Compaction gate and trigger builders (SJC 2610.20927, ACON, the corpus study's triggers, CL-W44-06's deletion arms)
consumers.action_changed: Score a gate's effect averaged over writer draws; read any history-based trigger against the $\sqrt{\rho_1}$ ceiling; stop reporting per-entry attribution from one draw as a property of the history.

consumers.class: Harness and product teams setting the compressor's sampling (Claude Code, Codex, OpenHands condenser, Pi)
consumers.action_changed: If the writer share is high, run the compressor at temperature 0 or ensemble $m$ draws and keep the intersection of entries; if low, leave it and spend replicates on the successor.
Treat the writer as a second instrument needing its own repeatability certificate, distinct from the replay certificate of the executable state.

papers.title: Does an Agent's History Tell You When Compaction Will Hurt? A Modest, Bounded Effect on the TRACE Paired-Replay Corpus
papers.trick: On 590 replayed AppWorld compaction boundaries, train triggers that predict post-compaction harm from pre-boundary history and compare them with a split-half replicate of the same boundary; the best trigger reaches AUROC 0.66 against a replicate yardstick of 0.72.
papers.did_not_do: Its replicate splits 'each boundary's PRE and POST rollouts into disjoint halves' with one summary per boundary (App. F), so it measures the successor-stage repeatability only (half-half correlation 0.40, Spearman-Brown full-sample reliability 0.57, task ICC 0.01); the writer stage is never re-drawn, the summary text is not in the release, and the authors write that 'the same numbers also support an attenuation reading' without the stage split that would say which stage attenuates.

papers.title: Parallel Context Compaction for Long-Horizon LLM Agent Serving
papers.trick: Compact a long history in parallel blocks instead of one blocking summarization call, so the operator controls summary volume and wall time at matched decode volume.
papers.did_not_do: Observes that 'both the amount of output tokens the model produces and the information it retains fluctuate substantially from run to run, making the agent's retained knowledge unpredictable across runs', which is the writer-stage repeatability stated as a serving problem; measures no downstream harm, no continuation, and no partition against the successor stage or between histories. Third: 2611.06545 (card) has writer reproducibility in pieces (1.2% versus 2.4% unsupported restrictions by writer; $K = 4$ successor runs) with one summary per source. Fourth: HSC-Bench 2610.36523 has receiver dependence (a reproducibility term on the successor side). Fifth: 2606.03463 replaces LLM summarisation with a deterministic pipeline because LLM summarisation 'introduces non-determinism', without measuring it. Pre-window precedents with their tricks: gauge R&R for agent scores (2610.00651, 2608.11323; the W42 S7xF9 record) and serving nondeterminism at temperature 0 (2602.07150).

nearest.verdict: Not made. Gauge R&R is imported for agent scores (W42 record), the successor-stage replicate exists (TRACE corpus study, summary fixed), writer reproducibility exists in pieces (2611.06545, HSC-Bench) and writer fluctuation is noted as a serving issue (2605.23296); no fetched source re-compacts the same history and partitions harm variance into writer, successor and between-history components (1 field-word hit, 13 lane-word hits). It is not a rename of the corpus study's replicate because that replicate holds the writer fixed by construction, and not a rename of CL-W43-14 / CL-W44-07 (run-to-run variance of agent scores) because the unit is the compaction boundary and the question is which stage of the handoff carries the dice.

reason_for_pick: S3 is the lane's live shape through card 2611.06545 and CL-W44-06; F9 is in Jacob's evaluable set and its agent-score import is already made (W42), so the question was the field's next step for the compaction stage specifically. The corpus study's replicate yardstick (2610.08722, read in full) turned out to hold the summary fixed, which makes the writer stage the unmeasured level of an otherwise nested design; 2611.06545's harness is public with a stochastic writer and executable outcomes, so the probe is a configuration change. Pairs with S3xF4 (closed as already-made) and the S8 row for the block.

scorecard.target_value: In print: 2610.08722 ('the same numbers also support an attenuation reading'; 'corpora should ship ordered actions, token counts, summary text and more replays'); 2605.23296 ('making the agent's retained knowledge unpredictable across runs'); 2611.06545's limitations (rule labeler recall unknown; one summary per source); 2611.05650's call for replay certificates. Who pays: compaction evaluators and gate builders whose labels are single draws; harness teams choosing the compressor's temperature.

floor.requires: steps 1-2 on the handoff-audit harness, one writer
floor.result: writer share under 0.10: a protocol footnote licensing single-summary labels and confirming TRACE's successor-only replicate as the right yardstick

middle.result: writer share at least 0.25 with the attenuation ceiling computed: compaction evaluations add a writer-replicate arm, per-boundary labels need $m \ge 3$, and the history-based trigger line is read against its ceiling; proper idea, lane-wide protocol change

ceiling.requires: step 4 on AppWorld plus one production-style compressor (another $400-800)
ceiling.result: the writer stage carries most of compaction harm variance across harnesses, so the recipe consequence (temperature 0 or $m$-draw intersection) is adopted by a public harness and 'compaction harm' papers report components by stage

relevance.routes: L4 all routes (a measurement with a protocol consequence); product teams directly (the compressor's temperature is a knob they own); L1 through the gauge-study register.
relevance.industry: Direct: every production compactor samples at some temperature and no one has measured what that costs.
relevance.jacob_edge: Direct: nested variance components, pooling rules and attenuation are statistics he can check by hand; the gauge analogy is his to say in a talk.
relevance.zero_where: L5, L3 (unless compaction frequency is the lever), the RL side of L2.

kill_probe.step: Step 1: 150 snapshots x 4 re-compactions x 3 continuations on the released handoff-audit harness; nested ANOVA with boundary-cluster bootstrap; writer share and $\rho_1$ reported.
kill_probe.criterion: dead if the writer share is under 0.10 with the interval's upper end under 0.20 on both writers; also dead as a ruler if fewer than 100 of 150 snapshots re-execute identically

scorecard.density_and_ownership: L4 is the densest lane (about one compaction paper a week). Occupied: the successor-stage replicate (2610.08722 App. F, summary fixed), writer reproducibility in pieces (2611.06545 by writer model; HSC-Bench by receiver), writer fluctuation as a serving issue (2605.23296), gauge R&R for agent scores (2610.00651, 2608.11323), serving nondeterminism (2602.07150). Unoccupied in every fetched source: re-compaction of the same history, the three-component partition of harm, the attenuation ceiling on history-based triggers, and the bias reading of per-writer unsupported-policy rates. Natural first movers: the TRACE authors (they hold the summaries) and the 2611.06545 author (the harness is theirs); the re-open test is asking them. Race window: about one paper a week against a 10-day probe on a public harness; proper-shaped from the solo position, golden only if the writer share is large across harnesses.
scorecard.why_now: 2610.08722 (2026-10-06) published the successor-only replicate yardstick and asked what corpora should ship; 2611.06545 (2026-11-04) released a harness with a stochastic writer at the developers' settings, snapshot replay and ledger-checked outcomes, so re-compaction is a configuration change; 2611.05650 (2026-11) made the replay certificate a norm, which the writer stage now needs separately; 2605.23296 (2026-05) documented the writer's run-to-run fluctuation without measuring its cost.
scorecard.register_and_what_it_is_not: Measurement register: a gauge study (three variance components and a bias reading) with a mechanism (harm inherits the writer's dice) and two consequences (replicate rule for labels; compressor temperature or ensemble). It is not a new compressor, not a trigger, not a harm predictor, and not a run-to-run variance study of agent scores (CL-W43-14, CL-W44-07): the unit is the compaction boundary and the question is which stage carries the variance.
